title: Sets: elements, subsets, union, intersection and complement
summary: Sort number cards into the ovals of a Venn diagram, write sets in braces, shade unions, intersections and differences, and count with the diagram.
guide: This studio follows Iran's Year 9 chapter on {{term:set}}s and Afghanistan's Year 7 chapter: {{term:element}}s, the {{term:venn-diagram}}, {{term:subset}}s, {{term:union}}, {{term:intersection}}, {{term:set-difference}}, the {{term:universal-set}}, the {{term:complement}}, and finite and infinite sets. In England, KS3 asks pupils to enumerate sets and unions and intersections with Venn diagrams.
Your child moves the cards by dragging them, or by tapping a card and then its place. With a keyboard, choose a card, then a button for a part of the diagram.

Common mistakes this studio works on: thinking the order of the elements matters, treating the {{term:empty-set}} as {{set:[0]}}, mixing up {{set:∈}} and {{set:⊆}}, thinking {{set:A − B}} is the same as {{set:B − A}}, and counting the overlap twice in {{set:A ∪ B}}.

engine.label-selected: Card {c} chosen. Now choose its place.
engine.label-layout: How should the ovals be drawn?
engine.row-school: every pupil in every school in the UK
engine.instruction-drag: Drag a card to its place, or tap the card and then its place.
engine.instruction-pick: Choose one answer for each row.
engine.instruction-nest: Sort the cards, then choose how to draw the ovals.
engine.instruction-shade: Tap a part of the diagram to shade it.
engine.instruction-count: Write the number in each part.

members-braces.title: Elements of a set
members-braces.prompt: The universal set U is the numbers 1 to 9. Set A is "the one-digit even numbers". Put the card of each {{term:element}} of A inside oval A. Then write A in braces: tap the cards under the braces.
members-braces.hint: An even number can be divided by 2. Write each element only once.
members-braces.success: Well done! {{set:A = [2, 4, 6, 8]}}. Every one-digit even number is an element of A.
members-braces.why: Are {{set:[2, 4, 6, 8]}} and {{set:[8, 6, 4, 2]}} the same set? Why?
members-braces.model: Yes. A set is fixed by its elements alone. The order we write them in does not matter, and writing an element twice does not make a new set. That is why we write each element once.

feedback.not-a-member: An odd number has gone into A. Odd numbers can't be divided by 2, so they are not in A. Put it outside the oval.
feedback.is-a-member: An even number is still outside. Find all the even numbers from 1 to 9.
feedback.write-empty: The diagram is right. Now write A in braces: tap the cards under the braces.
feedback.repeat: You wrote an element twice. In a set each element is written once: {{set:[2, 2, 4]}} is just {{set:[2, 4]}}. Tap the extra card inside the braces to take it out.
feedback.members-missing: An element of A is missing from the braces. Look at oval A.
feedback.members-extra: You wrote a number that is not inside oval A. Tap it to take it out.

element-or-subset.title: Element or subset?
element-or-subset.prompt: {{set:A = [2, 4, 6, 8]}}. Choose the right symbol for each row. {{set:∈}} means "is an element of" and is used for one element on its own. {{set:⊆}} means "is a {{term:subset}} of" and is used for a set.
element-or-subset.hint: 4 is a number, but {{set:[4]}} is a set with one element. {{set:∅}} is a set with no elements at all.
element-or-subset.success: Well done! {{set:4 ∈ A}} but {{set:[4] ⊆ A}}. The order of the elements does not matter, and the {{term:empty-set}} is not {{set:[0]}}.
element-or-subset.model: {{set:∅}} has no elements, but {{set:[0]}} has one element: the number zero. Zero is a number, not "nothing". So {{set:∅ ≠ [0]}}.

feedback.rows-unanswered: A row has no answer yet.
feedback.element-vs-subset: {{set:∈}} and {{set:⊆}} are mixed up. If the left side is a number on its own, we ask "is it an element?", so {{set:∈}}. If it is in braces, it is a set, and we ask "is it a subset?", so {{set:⊆}}.
feedback.order-matters: The order of the elements does not matter. Both sets have exactly 2 and 4, so they are equal.
feedback.empty-vs-zero: {{set:[0]}} is not empty: it has one element, zero. The {{term:empty-set}} has no elements.
feedback.five-odd: 5 is odd and is not in A, so {{set:5 ∉ A}}.
feedback.row-wrong: One row is not right. Look at the elements of A again.

subset-nest.title: A set inside another set
subset-nest.prompt: B is the one-digit even numbers and C is the one-digit multiples of 4. Sort the cards into the ovals. Then look at what is left in "only C", and choose the right way to draw the ovals.
subset-nest.hint: 4 and 8 are even and multiples of 4. Is there a multiple of 4 that is not even?
subset-nest.success: Well done! Every element of C is also in B, so C is a {{term:subset}} of B: {{set:C ⊆ B}}. In a {{term:venn-diagram}}, C is drawn inside B.
subset-nest.why: Why did we draw oval C inside oval B?
subset-nest.model: Because every multiple of 4 is even. The part "only C" had no elements, so all the elements of C are in B too. So {{set:C ⊆ B}}, and C is drawn inside B. It does not work the other way round: 2 is in B but not in C.

feedback.cards-left: Some cards are still outside the diagram. Put every card in its place.
feedback.in-both: This number is in B and in C. Put it in the overlap.
feedback.not-a-member: An odd number is neither even nor a multiple of 4, so it stays outside both ovals.
feedback.is-a-member: An even number is still outside the ovals.
feedback.two-not-multiple: 2 and 6 are even, but they are not multiples of 4. They go in "only B".
feedback.region-wrong: A card is in the wrong place. For each number ask: is it even? Is it a multiple of 4?
feedback.layout-wrong: The cards are right! Now look at "only C": it is empty. So all of C is inside B. Choose "C inside B".
feedback.subset-reversed: That's the wrong way round. B has elements that are not in C (2 and 6), so B does not fit inside C.
feedback.they-share: B and C have elements in common (4 and 8), so they are not apart.

union-intersection.title: Union and intersection
union-intersection.prompt: U is the numbers 1 to 10. A is the factors of 6 and B is the factors of 8. First shade the {{term:intersection}} {{set:A ∩ B}}. Then write the {{term:union}} {{set:A ∪ B}} in braces.
union-intersection.hint: The intersection is the elements in A and in B. The union is the elements in at least one of them; write the shared elements only once.
union-intersection.why: When you write {{set:A ∪ B}}, why do you write 1 and 2 only once?
union-intersection.model: 1 and 2 are in A and in B, but in a union each element appears once. If we just wrote the elements of A and then the elements of B, the overlap would be counted twice. That is why {{set:A ∪ B}} has six elements, not eight.

feedback.shade-empty: First shade {{set:A ∩ B}}: tap the right part of the diagram.
feedback.union-intersection: That is the union, not the intersection. {{set:A ∩ B}} is only the part where the two ovals overlap.
feedback.only-one-set: You shaded all of A. The intersection is only the elements of A that are also in B.
feedback.shade-missing: Not all of it is shaded. The intersection is the part where the two ovals overlap.
feedback.shade-extra: Too much is shaded. The intersection is only the part where the two ovals overlap.
feedback.write-empty: The shading is right. Now write {{set:A ∪ B}} in braces.
feedback.overlap-twice: You wrote 1 and 2 twice: once for A and once for B. In a union each element appears only once.
feedback.repeat: You wrote an element twice. Tap the extra card inside the braces to take it out.
feedback.wrote-intersection: That is {{set:A ∩ B}}. The union has all the elements of A and all the elements of B together.
feedback.members-missing: An element is missing. Every number inside at least one of the ovals is in the union.
feedback.members-extra: You wrote a number that is not in either oval.

difference-complement.title: Difference and complement
difference-complement.prompt: The same A and B. First shade {{set:A − B}}: the elements of A that are not in B. Then write the {{term:complement}} of A, {{set:A′}}: the elements of the {{term:universal-set}} U that are not in A.
difference-complement.hint: {{set:A − B}} starts with A and leaves out the overlap. For {{set:A′}}, don't forget the numbers outside both ovals.
difference-complement.why: Is {{set:A − B}} the same as {{set:B − A}}? Why?
difference-complement.model: No. {{set:A − B = [3, 6]}}: the elements of A that are not in B. But {{set:B − A = [4, 8]}}. With a difference the order matters, just as 5 − 3 is not the same as 3 − 5.

feedback.difference-reversed: That is {{set:B − A}}. {{set:A − B}} starts with A: the elements of A that are not in B.
feedback.only-vs-all: You shaded all of A. 1 and 2 are in B as well, so they are not in {{set:A − B}}.
feedback.difference-common: That is the overlap, {{set:A ∩ B}}. {{set:A − B}} leaves the overlap out.
feedback.shade-missing: Not all of it is shaded. Shade all of "only A".
feedback.shade-extra: Too much is shaded. {{set:A − B}} is only the part "only A".
feedback.write-empty: The shading is right. Now write {{set:A′}} in braces.
feedback.outside-missed: 4 and 8 are right, but 5, 7, 9 and 10 are not in A either. The complement is every element of U that is not in A, even those outside both ovals.
feedback.complement-not-b: That is B. 1 and 2 are in A, so they are not in {{set:A′}}. And the numbers outside the ovals are in {{set:A′}} too.
feedback.complement-not-difference: That is {{set:A − B}}. {{set:A′}} is the elements of U that are not in A.
feedback.repeat: You wrote an element twice. Tap the extra card to take it out.
feedback.members-missing: A number in U that is not in A is missing.
feedback.members-extra: You wrote a number that is in A; the complement of A does not have it.

count-overlap.title: Counting with a Venn diagram
count-overlap.prompt: A class has 20 pupils. 12 are in the football team (F), 8 are in the volleyball team (V), and 5 are in both teams. Write the number in each part of the diagram. Then say how many pupils are in at least one team.
count-overlap.hint: Start with the overlap: 5 pupils. 12 play football and 5 of them are in the overlap, so how many are in "only F"?
count-overlap.success: Well done! {{set:n(F ∪ V) = 7 + 5 + 3 = 15}}. You can also show the table to see the row and column totals.
count-overlap.why: Why is 12 + 8 = 20 not the number of pupils in a team?
count-overlap.model: Because the 5 pupils in both teams are counted in the 12 and again in the 8, so twice. We take them away once: 12 + 8 − 5 = 15. The diagram shows the same: 7 + 5 + 3 = 15. The other 5 pupils are in no team.

feedback.count-empty: One part is still empty. Write a number in all four parts, even outside the ovals.
feedback.only-vs-all: 12 and 8 are all the members of each team, including the 5 pupils in both. Take those 5 away for "only F" and "only V".
feedback.outside-missed: There are 20 pupils in the class. Those in no team go outside the ovals. How many are there?
feedback.count-wrong: One of the numbers is not right. All the parts together make 20; F makes 12 altogether and V makes 8.
feedback.empty: The diagram is right! Now type the answer: how many pupils are in at least one team?
feedback.overlap-twice: You counted the 5 pupils in the overlap twice. Add the numbers inside the ovals, each part once.
feedback.too-big: That's too many. Don't count the pupils who are in no team.
feedback.too-small: That's too few. Add "only F", "only V" and the overlap together.

finite-infinite.title: Finite or infinite?
finite-infinite.prompt: A set whose elements can be counted, with the counting coming to an end, is a {{term:finite-set}}. If the counting never ends, it is an {{term:infinite-set}}. Decide for each set.
finite-infinite.hint: Ask: does it have a last element? A very big set is still finite if the counting ends.
finite-infinite.success: Well done! The even numbers and the multiples of 5 never end, so they are infinite. The others are finite, however big they are.
finite-infinite.why: The set of every pupil in every school in the UK is very big. Why is it still finite?
finite-infinite.model: Because the pupils can be counted one by one and the counting does end, even if it takes a very long time. But the even numbers have no last element: after every even number there is a bigger one.

feedback.rows-unanswered: A set has no answer yet.
feedback.big-not-infinite: Big is not the same as infinite. This set has a last element, so counting it ends.
feedback.no-last: This set has no last element: however far you go, there is a bigger one. So it is infinite.
feedback.row-wrong: One answer is not right. For each set ask: does it have a last element?
